issues.legal_issue: Expenditure incurred to remove an obstruction to an existing mining business is revenue expenditure when it does not acquire a capital asset.
material_facts: The business operator held a mining lease covering the land beneath a railway area and had the right to extract minerals from the leased land.
Railway tracks, a station, yards and buildings obstructed mining operations in part of the leased area.
After failing to remove the railway occupation through litigation, the operator agreed with the relevant authorities and other parties to share the cost of relocating the railway establishment.
The operator paid its share of the relocation cost to remove the obstruction and enable mining in the leased area; it acquired no new mineral right or capital asset through the payment.
After relocation, the operator mined the previously obstructed area and supplied the extracted gypsum to a customer.
issues.conclusion: The relocation payment was revenue expenditure and deductible. The appeal was allowed, the High Court's order was set aside, and the Tribunal's order allowing the deduction was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, and the corresponding principle in section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, the character of expenditure depends on the nature of the business, the purpose and commercial effect of the expenditure, and the nature of the right or advantage obtained. Where a business already has the right to operate, expenditure incurred in the course of business to remove a restriction, obstruction or disability is on revenue account if it does not acquire a capital asset, even if it benefits the business. The enduring-benefit test is not conclusive. The Court applied and affirmed the approach in Empire Jute Company v. Commissioner of Income Tax and relied on Gotan Lime Syndicate v. Commissioner of Income Tax, M.A. Jabbar v. Commissioner of Income Tax, and Commissioner of Inland Revenue v. Carron Company. It referred to Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax and K.T.M.T.M. Abdul Kayoom v. Commissioner of Income Tax for the fact-specific nature of the inquiry, explained the test in British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd. v. Atherton, and distinguished R.B. Seth Moolchand Suganchand v. Commissioner of Income Tax because that case concerned obtaining rights to initiate mining activity rather than removing an obstruction to an existing business.

rule.if: tax_deduction_dispute and existing_mining_right and expenditure_in_course_of_business and railway_obstruction and payment_removed_obstruction and no_new_capital_asset

predicates.tax_deduction_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether expenditure incurred in a business is deductible in computing taxable income.
predicates.existing_mining_right: The business operator already held the right to mine the land where operations were obstructed.
predicates.expenditure_in_course_of_business: The business operator incurred the expenditure while carrying on its existing business.
predicates.railway_obstruction: Railway infrastructure on the leased land obstructed the business operator's mining operations.
predicates.payment_removed_obstruction: The business operator paid toward relocating the railway infrastructure so it could carry on mining operations in the obstructed area.
predicates.no_new_capital_asset: The payment did not give the business operator a new right to minerals or any other capital asset.

issues.definition: When a tax-deduction dispute concerns expenditure made in an existing mining business to remove a railway obstruction, and the payment acquires no capital asset, the expenditure is revenue expenditure and deductible.
